long_biography.plain_text:
Sergei Shmotev's collecting helped Ural stone carvers move from small decorative figures to ambitious sculptural compositions. He worked closely with craftsmen as their pieces became more intricate, while his collection expanded from edged weapons into painting and carved stone. His son Alexander joined him in establishing a family arts foundation in 2019.

The foundation brought private holdings into public exhibitions and worked with the Yekaterinburg Museum of Fine Arts to open a centre devoted to stone-carving history. Visitors can study the work of Alexei Denisov-Uralsky and then try stoneworking themselves in a basement workshop equipped with grinding discs and drills.
